raw_response:
I'm 58 this year, and I've been working these fields since I was 18 — forty years. My old man passed me the knowledge, and now my son helps when he can, though he's mostly working construction over in Handan. There's four of us in the house: me, my wife, my son, and my daughter-in-law. We got 28.1 mu total, which isn't big but it's enough to keep us busy and put food on the table. I finished middle school, so I can read the fertilizer bags and understand what the extension technician says, but to be honest, I trust what I've seen with my own eyes more than what some young fellow reads out of a book.

This year, I'm sticking with what I know. The extension guy keeps talking about reducing fertilizer, saying 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough for wheat, but last year I tried cutting back on a small plot and the yield dropped — I got maybe 400 jin per mu instead of my usual 480. That cost me more than the fertilizer I saved. So this year I'm doing what I've always done, maybe a touch more. I can't afford a bad year. My son's job isn't steady, and we need the grain income to cover the household expenses.

Here's how I'm thinking about each crop:

**Wheat (18 mu):** This is my backbone. I plant Jinmai 47 in the first week of October — it's reliable, and I know how it behaves. I buy new certified seed every third year; this year I'm using seed I saved from two years ago, treated with fungicide. Before planting, I'll spread about 50 kg per mu of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) as base dressing — that's what I've done for twenty years. Then at green-up in March, I'll broadcast about 10 kg per mu of urea, and at jointing stage another 8 kg if the wheat looks a bit yellow. Total nitrogen comes to about 18 kg per mu, a bit more than the extension recommendation, but I sleep better that way. I'll irrigate three times: once before winter to help establishment, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. The electricity for pumping keeps getting more expensive — about 35 yuan per irrigation now — but skipping the jointing water is gambling, and I don't gamble. For pests, I spray once for aphids in spring and maybe a fungicide if powdery mildew shows up. I expect about 480 jin per mu if the weather cooperates.

**Maize (18 mu, same land):** Right after wheat harvest, around June 10th to 15th, I plant summer maize. The window is brutal — sometimes only four or five days. I hire a tractor with a precision planter, costs me 40 yuan per mu, because at 58 I can't plant 18 mu by hand in that heat and humidity. I use Zhengdan 958 hybrid seed, about 4 kg per mu, costs around 50 yuan per mu. At planting I put down about 40 kg per mu of compound fertilizer in the row. Then at the big trumpet stage I'll side-dress with about 15 kg per mu of urea. Total N is roughly 16 kg per mu. I irrigate twice — once when it's tasseling and once at grain filling — though if the summer rains are good I might skip the second one. Maize has been giving me about 550 jin per mu the last few years. I spray for armyworm once if I see damage.

**Cotton (5 mu):** I keep this on the western plot. My wife handles most of the picking, but last year her wrists hurt so bad we hired two women from the next village for 8 days at 80 yuan per day. I'll plant in late April with local seed, about 2 kg per mu. I put down 30 kg per mu of compound fertilizer at planting, then urea at flowering and boll-setting — total about 12 kg N per mu. I irrigate twice, and I spray three or four times for bollworms and aphids; those pests get worse every year. Cotton prices have been decent lately, so I'm keeping the 5 mu despite the backbreaking labor. Expecting about 250 jin of seed cotton per mu.

**Spinach (2 mu):** Near the house on the good black soil. I plant in late September after clearing the summer weeds, and harvest in batches from November through March. It's mainly for family eating — my wife makes great spinach noodles — but I sell the surplus at the village market for pocket money. I put down some well-rotted manure and about 10 kg of urea per mu. Two irrigations, that's it. Very little work, maybe family labor only.

**Soybean (1 mu):** On the sandy east corner where nothing else grows well. I plant in late June, after the early rains. Soybean doesn't need much nitrogen, so I just put down 20 kg per mu of superphosphate at planting. Maybe one irrigation if July is dry. I harvest in October and sell to the oil mill in town. Low input, low output, but it uses land that would otherwise sit idle.

**Mungbean (1 mu):** Next to the soybean on that sandy plot. Planted in early June, harvested in August-September. My wife sprouts some for selling at market, and we eat the rest. Like soybean, I just add some phosphate fertilizer, about 15 kg per mu. One irrigation if needed. Quick crop, doesn't tie up the land long.

**Chrysanthemum (1.1 mu):** My wife's project — Hangbaiju, the medicinal kind. I transplant seedlings in May, and she harvests the flowers in October-November, dries them on the kang, and a buyer from Anhui comes by once a year to collect. Doesn't bring much, maybe 2,000 yuan total after all the work, but it keeps her busy and the money is hers to manage. I put some organic fertilizer down, maybe spray once for aphids. It's on the plot near the house so she can watch it.

**Money and labor:** I'm watching costs closely. Fertilizer prices went up again, and diesel for the pumps isn't cheap. I have about 10,000 yuan I can put into inputs this year without borrowing, and I want to keep 2,000 in reserve for emergencies — my wife's medicine, or if the tractor breaks. My son comes back for wheat harvest and maize planting, maybe 10 days total. The rest of the year it's me and my wife. For the heavy peaks — wheat harvest, maize planting, and cotton picking — I'll hire labor or machines. I'd rather spend 800 yuan on hired help than ruin my back.

Altogether, I'm looking at spending about 9,850 yuan on seeds, fertilizer, chemicals, irrigation, and hired labor. That's a lot, but if wheat and maize both give me decent yields, I'll clear enough to get through the year and maybe fix the roof.
